articles.title: How the AI boom might really end: 5 scenarios
articles.reason: 涵盖 AI product & news、Startup & business
articles.summary: With chip stocks on their longest losing streak since 2008 and Anthropic heading for IPO, five ways the AI boom could end - and why I think the value is real but may not flow to the people putting the money in.
articles.full_text:
With the Anthropic IPO gathering pace - and chip stocks just posting their longest losing streak since 2008 amid worries about AI debt , I thought it'd be worth writing up some of my thoughts I've put together while thinking through what may happen.

By no means is this meant to be exhaustive - just a list of what I think is the most interesting to think through.

Before I dive into the scenarios, while I'm sure there are going to be failures and mispricing of asset classes - like any huge investment wave - I think it's worth saying that unlike many bubbles there is an enormous amount of value being created.

In essence, I think this is the first time capital can be turned into intelligence.

You buy (or borrow money for) GPUs, you get tokens out which represent a growing share of professional service work.

I'm certainly biased as a software engineer by trade - the models just get better and better at coding and it's humbling to see it do my previous tasks so quickly and increasingly better than I can do them.

And unlike (say) the dotcom boom, which was arguably directionally correct, but far too early, we're seeing mass adoption and huge revenues being generated, far quicker than in the late 90s.

So thinking through this, I'd group the scenarios into two categories.

Firstly, AI itself doesn't deliver the value promised or gets stopped by external factors.

I think these are worth thinking through.

The other category - and potentially more likely - is that AI works well, but the value doesn't flow to the people that are putting the money in.

I think this is where the unwinding could happen, and arguably is already showing up.

Group 1: AI disappoints or gets stopped Models stop getting any better While it's hard to argue that the models as is aren't "good" at specific tasks now, it may well be that we hit a scaling wall.

Increasing amounts of capex is pumped into model training, but the results are incrementally better.

This leads to a "hard" wall on progress until another architecture or approach potentially comes along.

This one I'd discount for now.

We're seeing no signs of progress slowing, and we're seeing very fast advancement in capabilities.

And even if this did happen, most organisations and people aren't using anywhere near their full power.

The one watch out though which is a bit more insidious is that the models continue getting better at specific tasks, but start regressing badly in others.

I feel Opus 5 was a good example of this - better at coding, but produced infuriatingly hard-to-read prose.

Perhaps we'll see models more focused at specific tasks if this gets harder to mitigate (much like the Codex series of GPT models, which then got unified back into the main GPT models).

Alignment risks The other major risk with AI is that it ends up doing something bad in the real world.

We've already seen the Hugging Face incident as a 'warning shot'.

But there are far more catastrophic risks at play - for example, shutting down national infrastructure, or hacking a major financial institution that results in systemic risk across markets.

Or, it goes full Skynet.

There is no doubt this would cause enormous political upheaval that would lead to very rapid and severe backlash.

Where the industry goes after that is hard to see - potentially progress gets frozen, resulting in far fewer orders for GPUs.

On the other hand, it's hard for me to see a globally coordinated moratorium on AI given the breakneck competition between (primarily) the US and China.

If it happened in China, is the US likely to follow suit?

Or would it, instead, be blamed on "defective Chinese" models, and the US continues as is?

Equally, if it happens in the US, does China pause or see this as a once in a generation opportunity to leap ahead?

I think we are getting dangerously close to an incident that may cause some sort of significant pullback in AI spending.

It's certainly hard to predict, and the severity matters a lot - along with human impact.

Datacentre ban Slightly less science fiction-y would be widespread local or political opposition to datacentre rollouts causing a very widespread pause on new capacity coming on stream.

While this is certainly happening - I have a suspicion this could be one of the key battlelines for the 2028 US election cycle - it again would have to be a global ban to have any significant effect.

If the US does a ban, projects and investments would quickly shift to other jurisdictions.

And I'm almost certain that China would not even entertain any sort of ban like this, which again adds a geopolitical angle to it.

Would the US really want to go ahead with a national ban when China already has a commanding lead in electricity capacity (if not semiconductors).

As such, I can't see this having a great effect on the deployment as a whole.

The real weakness lies in financing these deals.

Much like Ørsted needed a $9.4bn rights issue after US stop-work orders on its offshore wind projects spooked its financing, we could quickly see a domino effect of financing failures caused by it.

Group 2: AI works, but the capex holders don't capture the value Open weights get so good they collapse margins I think this is the standout from where I see the risk and something I've been writing about for a while now.

We're in the middle of a brutal inference price war - if you want to read more read my other recent article .

This is largely caused by open weights models crossing the threshold of being "good enough" for many tasks.

Anthropic releasing Haiku 5.5 at a huge discount - 90% cheaper on short context windows - means that for shorter, bulk tasks, Anthropic & OpenAI are actually as cheap as, or cheaper than, comparable open weights models.

This doesn't apply for longer agentic tasks with Haiku - the price jumps 5x once you go over 100K tokens of context.

Interestingly, OpenAI is far more aggressive here: GPT-6 Luna only goes up 1.5-2x, and only past 272K tokens.

But I was surprised recently to find that no reputable inference provider offers comparable open weights models (e.g.

DeepSeek) at any significant discount to Haiku and Luna, which is an enormous change from where we were at the start of the year, where the frontier labs were charging 10-20x more than open weight models.

How much this cannibalises their more expensive models is up for debate.

They've done the pricing in such a way that for longer agentic tasks, open weight models are still very attractive.

But the perpetual price drops must be having some impact on margins, even if it does lead to them (re)taking market share from open weights competitors.

So the hope is that they continue cutting prices, but revenue/token growth outstrips that.

It is certainly possible - but it shows how fast this market switches that we've now got frontier labs offering this inference at all .

The wildcard I would keep though is that while the open weights labs have kept pace, we can't rule out the frontier labs' ability to throw a lot of compute and brainpower at new models.

Opus 5.5, for example, is an excellent model for more demanding tasks.

And the Chinese labs are clearly short of hardware and facing new export restrictions from the Chinese government.

Huge efficiency breakthroughs Note that the previous scenario, while catastrophic for the frontier labs if this compression continues, arguably increases demand for semiconductors, memory and the related supply chain.

But another risk is that if there are huge efficiency breakthroughs, either through hardware or software/model improvements.

This is what killed the telecoms boom in the early 2000s - it wasn't so much that bandwidth growth stopped, but the efficiency of fibre optics far outpaced the demands.

So far we've seen a lot of innovation on the model side, but hardware has struggled to keep pace.

Discounting all the hype stats that Nvidia etc put out for each new generation [1] , underlying tokens/watt - the best figure to watch - is improving far slower than the headlines suggest.

The model efficiency improvements have been pretty amazing to watch.

But so far, this has all been put into longer context windows (enabling longer running agentic tasks) and have enabled some of the price decreases we've seen.

But, there is a world where a new hardware or software approach does lead, much like DWDM fibre back in the 2000s, to efficiency running far, far ahead of token growth, even taking Jevons paradox into account.

My gut says that token demand is growing so fast, and will continue to grow so fast that it will consume all efficiency gains in the near future.

The key way to track this I think is not looking at some of the "token cost indexes" that get posted about - this doesn't adjust for the exponential growth in demand - but instead look at the cost of GPUs on the spot market.

If we start seeing big , broad drops across all compute types, then that's a clear sign that supply and demand is starting to reach equilibrium and this scenario is starting to play out.

Conclusion There are no doubt many risks to the AI "economy", and it's always easy to point to whatever one is making the most news.

But to me the real question is whether AI progress is turning into tangible value.

Right now - for me, and many others, the answer is a resounding yes.

Token consumption is going through the roof, because as models get better more and more tasks can be executed with AI.

And I still think early adopters that are pushing agentic workflows comprise a small single-digit percentage of the professional services market as a whole.

But this doesn't mean that the labs making and serving those models take the benefit.

History is littered with huge technological advancements which went to consumer surplus , not whoever bet the most capital.

And my view is that's what we are seeing right now.

The frontier labs are in serious peril of losing margin, and therefore market valuation, to open weights competitors.

The important point though is that the frontier labs do not make up the whole market.

Tokens need compute, memory and power whether it's a frontier lab or open weights.

I see endless analysis of OpenAI vs Anthropic revenue figures.

What's far more important to the AI ecosystem is overall revenues.

And as the market continues to fragment, it's harder and harder to join that together.

Unless AI does hit a wall, open weights may mean the end of the boom in frontier labs valuations.

But the underlying supply chains may be doing better than ever.

Which is why I think the market has this week backwards.

Chip stocks are being punished just as TSMC reports record revenue and says AI demand still exceeds supply .

The one caveat is leverage.

So much of this buildout is debt-funded that even small changes can unwind far faster, and far more completely, than they should.

CoreWeave's credit default swaps hit distressed levels this week on a hot inflation print and a viral chart - not because anyone stopped wanting GPUs.

If the AI boom ends, I don't think it ends with fewer tokens.

It ends with the same tokens - or far more - flowing to far more people at far lower margins.

Nvidia's headline generation-on-generation numbers mostly come from dropping precision (FP8 to FP4), not from the silicon getting more efficient.

Halving precision roughly doubles throughput on the same hardware, but you're trading accuracy for speed, and most production inference still runs at FP8 or BF16.

Compare like-for-like at FP8 and H100 to Vera Rubin is roughly 2.7x per watt over three generations - about 1.5x a generation.

Over the same period power per GPU went from ~700W to ~2,300W, so more than half the per-GPU gain is simply drawing more power through bigger, multi-die packages.

Moore's law is slowing, and there's a hard limit to how far you can cut precision.

Once both run out, the tok/watt gains have to come from somewhere else. ↩︎ If you found this useful, I send a newsletter every month with all my posts.

articles.full_text:
AI Report Tech Websites are closing their doors to AI agents OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you.

But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen.

OpenAI, Meta, and Google want AI agents to do everything for you.

But popular services on the web aren’t letting that happen. by Emma Roth Oct 17, 2026, 1:00 PM UTC Link Share Gift Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Getty Images Emma Roth is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.

Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Autonomous agents are the hottest thing in AI.

OpenAI, Meta, Google, Instinct, and others promise their agents can scour the internet on your behalf, doing anything from booking a dinner reservation and cleaning out your inbox to buying new shoes.

But what happens when the rest of the internet won’t play nice?

In recent weeks, users of services like Meta’s Muse, xAI’s Grok, OpenAI’s Dots, and Instinct have reported blocks preventing their AI agents from performing tasks across top websites.

Yelp told TechCrunch that it only allows AI agents that pay for its data licensing program, while Delta Air Lines is preventing them from booking tickets on behalf of users.

JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have also confirmed that they’re blocking AI agents from accessing accounts due to security concerns.

Some users say sites that previously worked with their AI agent are no longer accessible, including Cars.com and Amtrak , suggesting other companies could be quietly blocking them.

Amazon was already fighting off AI agents last year when it banned Perplexity’s agentic shopping feature and sued the AI startup , raising legal and practical questions about the future of agents on the web.

At the time, Amazon claimed it “repeatedly requested” that Perplexity stop allowing its AI agents to shop on its website, adding that third-party companies that purchase items on behalf of customers “should operate openly and respect service provider decisions whether or not to participate.” Perplexity responded by pointing out that Amazon doesn’t want AI agents roaming its platform because it won’t get as many human eyeballs in front of its ads — which is an actual issue for the ecommerce giant.

The AI startup likened its AI agent to an extension of the user, arguing that Amazon “does not believe in your right to hire labor, to have an assistant or an employee acting on your behalf.” While a judge later ordered Perplexity to stop its AI agents from shopping on its website, an appeals court overturned this ruling in August .

Amazon has since filed an amended complaint .

Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems This ongoing legal battle didn’t stop OpenAI, Meta, and Google from rolling out agents of their own.

But they’re dealing with the same problems as Perplexity.

Muse, Meta’s deceptively cute AI assistant, most recently faced the wrath of Amazon , which said its “continued access” violates its site policies.

There are reports of xAI’s Grok , Instinct’s AI agent, and OpenAI’s Dots being unable to use Amazon as well. xAI owner Elon Musk responded by saying that maybe he “should start a competitor to Amazon.” The more places bots struggle to access, the greater the questions about how useful they are. “Does this impact the perceived value of the Anthropics and the OpenAIs?

I would say absolutely,” Chris Canal, the CEO of the AI safety evaluator EquiStamp, tells The Verge . “One of the claims is that they’re going to permeate every aspect of our lives and be able to do anything that we could do online.

If there are companies that are actively working to make that not happen, there are just fewer useful things the agents can do.” Meta responded to instances of websites blocking Muse in a post earlier this month . “Turning away a personal agent means turning away the customer behind it,” the company says. “We’d rather work with businesses to address the underlying concerns than see them lose that customer.” Instead of trying to fight Amazon, the company has partnered with retailers like Walmart, Gap, Sephora, Best Buy, and others, allowing Muse to shop on their sites.

At the same time, Shopify has also opened its network of storefronts to AI agents.

The Verge reached out to OpenAI and Google with requests for comments on the roadblocks their AI agents are facing but didn’t immediately hear back.

Instinct declined to comment.

Even if websites aren’t banning AI agents outright, agents may still be clashing with anti-bot systems, which have become ubiquitous across the web.

Reports on Reddit suggest that Google is blocking some accounts that use Muse due to “suspicious activity,” while others have reported issues checking out on Walmart despite its Meta partnership. “There are all kinds of things that are set up not even to block agents, but to block in general bots or programs that are trying to scam or hack,” Canal adds. “These AI agents trigger those same safeguards.” Related Friends don’t let friends feed their data to AI agents Instinct was the buzziest AI agent around — can it survive Muse?

The web architecture provider Cloudflare has also played a role in helping sites clamp down on unwanted AI visitors.

After introducing a one-click block for AI crawlers in 2025, Cloudflare began blocking crawlers that simultaneously scrape websites for both search indexing and AI training.

The move is part of Cloudflare’s efforts to save the web from an influx of AI bots, which is putting a strain on internet infrastructure and wreaking havoc on email inboxes, and which could eventually make it even harder than it already is to compete against bots when purchasing concert tickets, booking reservations, or trying to get ahold of certain products.

While these blocks may help keep some AI agents and bots out of a website, Canal says they will ultimately make the web more “annoying” to use as more sites roll out interfaces to confirm you’re not a robot. “We could see them on a simple grocery shopping website soon, where you’re having to jump through a bunch of hoops to prove that you’re a human using the computer or your phone.” Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.

articles.title: Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings
articles.summary: The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year.
articles.full_text:
The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.

Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to  “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.” One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude  and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.” In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.

Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.

The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it’s up 16% for technical contributors.

The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.” Topics AI , Anthropic When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission .

This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

Anthony Ha Anthony Ha is TechCrunch’s weekend editor.

Previously, he worked as a tech reporter at Adweek, a senior editor at VentureBeat, a local government reporter at the Hollister Free Lance, and vice president of content at a VC firm.

He lives in New York City.

articles.title: Replit makes OpenAI its default over Anthropic, CEO says
articles.summary: Over the weekend, Masad clarified that OpenAI would replace Anthropic as its default model provider. Claude will still be available to customers on the platform.
articles.full_text:
Replit, the AI coding platform that has become a favorite of startup founders and developers, is no longer working with Anthropic, the company’s CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad said Thursday while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt .

Masad said the decision was made for a number of different reasons, including cost.

Replit announced a partnership with OpenAI in August, but there was never any indication that it was no longer partnering with Anthropic.  “I think ChatGPT is better now,” Masad said, adding that the company uses an internal benchmark to help assess metrics like performance. “We publish a public benchmark as well, and consistently, Sol and Astra perform better on building vibe-coded applications from scratch.

It was a decision based on both cost, partnership, and performance.

And for all these reasons, we just felt like they were a better partner for now.” It seems, however, that Anthropic hasn’t been completely cut out of Replit, which sells a cloud-based software development platform where users can develop and deploy apps directly from inside their browser.  After Disrupt, Masad clarified that customers can still access Anthropic models on the platform, but that OpenAI’s ChatGPT is now the default.

This shift could significantly reduce Replit’s spend with Anthropic since most customers stick with the default rather than selecting a model themselves.

Prior to striking a deal with OpenAI, Replit relied on Anthropic’s Claude models to run its platform.

That partnership was said to have helped the company grow its revenue significantly, and Masad noted on stage that Replit had been, until recently, a top-five customer of Anthropic’s. “Replit remains model agnostic,” Masad told TechCrunch over the weekend. “Our users can choose Anthropic’s Claude or other supported models…OpenAI is now our preferred partner for powering Replit Agent, based on performance, economics, and the strength of our partnership.” Masad’s comments on stage were rejected by insiders familiar with the partnership between the Anthropic and Replit, however.

One person familiar, who asked not to be named, said the partnership was still in place.

There is evidence on the company’s website , blog posts, and social media posts that Replit was promoting Anthropic products as recently as a few weeks ago.

For instance, a blog post in late September cites Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 and Claude Fable 5.1 as models running in Replit Agent’s production environment.

Around the same time, one of Replit’s product employees posted on X about using Anthropic’s flagship model Opus 5.5 and promoting its capabilities.

Masad also shared insights about the company’s growth while onstage at Disrupt, noting that enterprise is starting to provide a larger slice of revenue. “We’re not sharing ARR numbers just yet, but in terms of growth, like, I would say, enterprise was like 2% of revenue last year,” Masad said. “This year, I would say like 15% of our revenue is enterprise contracts, and more than 50% of our revenue is B2B.” Backstage, Masad told TechCrunch that he expects more than half of Replit’s revenue to come from enterprise and government customers in 2027.

Masad also commented on the necessity for good AI safety measures. “In the same way that us humans need a certain environment to work — you need a nice office, maybe nice good food in the office, air-conditioning, computer — agents need a habitat for them to exist and do good work,” he said. “So that habitat has good orchestration, good error recovery, good safety and security and sandboxing, good networking, good identity and authorization.

And once you figure all of that out, then you can deploy AI safely.” This article was originally published on October 16 at 2:22 pm PT.

It has been updated to include more context around Replit’s partnerships with Anthropic and OpenAI.

Its title has been updated, as well.
